subject: Egress naming, IP zone mapping & firewall guidance for Private Endpoint pilot
messages:

Subject: Request: egress zone naming & IP mapping for private endpoint pilot

Hi Jasmine —

Thanks again for the demo last week. We're kicking off the internal network prep for the Private Endpoint pilot and the network team asked for a concise mapping they can use in firewall rules and change tickets. Specifically we're looking for:

- A canonical list of egress "zones" (control plane, model inference, telemetry, updates) with the recommended destination hostnames/IPs and ports
- Guidance on whether we should rely on DNS allowlisting only, or a combination of DNS + static IP allowlist (we use a strict outbound policy)
- Any suggestions for handling ephemeral/elastic IPs and updates (e.g., update cadence or a proxy pattern)
- Minimal sample firewall rules / security-group snippets we can drop into a runbook

If you have a one-pager or CSV we can import into our change system that would be ideal. We're aiming to submit a change ticket on Monday and would like to avoid a round of redlines.

Thanks —
Alex
Network Security Lead
Acme Health

From: Jasmine Liu <jasmine.liu@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Chen <alex.chen@acmehealth.com>
Cc: security@acmehealth.com
Date: Sat, 15 Aug 2026 17:45:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Request: egress zone naming & IP mapping for private endpoint pilot

Hi Alex —

Appreciate the clear ask. I've put together an initial mapping and a few operational recommendations below; attaching a CSV you can import and a short playbook for firewall teams. This is deliberately conservative — we can tighten once the pilot traffic profile is observed.

High-level egress zones (recommended):

1) control-plane.api (control plane egress)
   - Purpose: control-plane telemetry, heartbeats, route/fallbacks (non-content)
   - Preferred: allow by FQDN (control.redwood.ai) + mTLS (when private deployments enable it)
   - Ports: 443 (HTTPS), 8443 (if customer NATs/port-translation)

2) inference.api (model tokenized egress)
   - Purpose: model variant downloads, fallback calls to lightweight hosted replicas (rare), and prompt-based non-customer-data telemetry (if enabled)
   - Preferred: DNS allowlist for model hostnames + a proxy (recommended) for accounting and IP stability
   - Ports: 443

3) telemetry.metrics (metrics & logs)
   - Purpose: metrics, alerting, traces (to configured sinks)
   - Preferred: explicit hostnames/IPs + TLS; consider separate outbound path to avoid throttling with inference traffic
   - Ports: 443, 9529 (if using custom collectors)

4) software.updates (maintenance & image pulls)
   - Purpose: OS/agent updates, artifact downloads during provisioning
   - Preferred: allowlist by IP ranges for package hosts or route via a controlled proxy/VPN; schedule maintenance windows
   - Ports: 80/443, certain registry ports (if self-hosted caches used)

Operational recommendations:

- DNS-first, IP-second: Where possible, reference FQDNs in your policies (SNI-aware allowlist). If your environment mandates IP-only rules, use the attached CSV but plan for weekly cadence updates.
- Edge proxy pattern: Run an internal egress proxy (transparent or explicit) that front-ends Redwood egress traffic. The proxy provides consistent egress IPs, central TLS inspection (optional), and observability. We recommend a single HA pair per AZ.
- mTLS for control plane: For control-plane traffic, enable mTLS to ensure identity and make firewall rules more permissive at the IP layer while enforcing auth at the TLS layer.
- Ephemeral IPs: For any ephemeral model-hosting pools, prefer proxying. If you must allow direct IPs, subscribe to our weekly IP CSV and automate change ingestion.
- Minimum firewall snippets (drop-in examples in playbook):
   - Allow outbound to control.redwood.ai:443 (SNI match)
   - Allow outbound to telemetry.redwood.ai:443 to the metrics collector CIDR
   - Allow outbound to 0.0.0.0/0:443 only via egress-proxy (10.0.0.5) for inference flows

Attachments included: egress-ip-zone-mapping.csv (columns: zone,host,cidr,ports,notes), redwood-firewall-playbook-v1.pdf (playbook and sample rules).

Next steps:
- If acceptable, I can schedule a 30-min runthrough with your network team tomorrow to walk the CSV and recommended ACLs.
- Laura and Ben on my side will be available to propose the minimal rule set we typically ship for pilots.

Thanks —

Jasmine Liu

Subject: Re: Request: egress zone naming & IP mapping for private endpoint pilot

Hi Alex / team —

Adding a couple of concrete policy snippets we hand to ops for pilot installs. These are intentionally minimal and assume the customer runs an outbound proxy at 10.0.0.5. If you do not run a proxy, we'll provide a variant that lists IP CIDRs instead.

Security-group example (AWS-style; replace CIDRs as needed):
- Outbound rule: dst=10.0.0.5:3128 (egress-proxy), proto=TCP, description="Redwood inference -> egress proxy"
- Outbound rule: dst=control.redwood.ai:443, proto=TCP, description="Control plane (mTLS preferred)"
- Outbound rule: dst=telemetry.redwood.ai:443, proto=TCP, description="Metrics & traces"

iptables example (edge NAT host allowing only proxy and control):
- iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp -d 10.0.0.5 --dport 3128 -j ACCEPT
- iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp -d control.redwood.ai --dport 443 -m comment --comment "control plane" -j ACCEPT
- iptables -A OUTPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j DROP  # all other direct HTTPS outbound blocked

Notes:
- If you need TLS inspection, place it at the proxy and keep control-plane mTLS to preserve identity.
- We recommend a weekly sync process: our IP CSV is published Friday UTC; configure your change system to consume it during a maintenance window.

Ben — can you confirm the NAT/proxy HA guidance (IP failover approach) and add the recommended healthcheck ports?

Laura Bennett
Platform Security, Redwood Inference
laura.bennett@redwood.ai
